documents: Mahan et al. 2023, Applied Geochemistry 148, 105519 (published paper, PDF)

entry.evidence: This case study was conducted to determine the efficacy of Cu isotopes for vectoring to ore using a known sediment-hosted Cu deposit

steps.action: Frame the need for cheap exploration methods able to detect Cu ore under cover, given falling discovery rates and the limits of geophysics and trace-metal hydrogeochemistry.
steps.quote: call for novel, time- and cost-effective mineral exploration methods

steps.action: Take from prior work the expectation that oxidative weathering and adsorption produce a bulls-eye of heavy Cu isotope enrichment in waters near Cu ore.
steps.quote: the generation of a bulls-eye trend of heavy Cu isotope enrichment

steps.action: Identify the gap: the Cu isotope vector has been shown for porphyry, exotic and IOCG deposits but never tested on a sediment-hosted deposit.
steps.quote: have not been applied to any known sediment-hosted copper deposits as ground truth

steps.action: Design a ground-truth test at the known Mount Isa deposit using existing monitoring bores proximal and distal to ore, a tailings dam sample, and ore chalcopyrite from two drill cores.
steps.quote: groundwater samples from environmental monitoring bores (18 bores, 1 tailings dam water sample) proximal and distal to the world-class Mount Isa Cu–Zn–Pb deposit

steps.action: Collect purged and filtered groundwater with field parameters (depth, pH, T, dO, EC) over three 2020 sessions, purify Cu by ion exchange and measure δ65Cu by MC-ICP-MS with sample-standard bracketing.
steps.quote: Groundwater samples were collected by the Environmental Department at Mount Isa Mines (MIM) in 2020 over three field sessions

steps.action: Check analytical quality with duplicate analyses, full procedural replicates for about 1 in 4 samples, and BHVO-2 and 1838 penny standards compared with literature values.
steps.quote: both standard values from the current work are in excellent agreement with literature data

steps.action: Measure 12 chalcopyrite samples from two drill cores in or above the main ore body to set a baseline deposit δ65Cu (average 0.00‰).
steps.quote: The total average Cu isotope composition for the main mineralization of the Mt Isa Cu–Zn–Pb deposit is 0.00‰

steps.action: Use agreement between groundwater duplicates to confirm that Cu purification was adequate even for high-NaCl waters.
steps.quote: good agreement and low analytical uncertainties confirm sufficient purification of Cu prior to isotopic analyses

steps.action: Set an EC threshold of 5000 μS/cm2 from literature benchmarks to flag and exclude industrially impacted bores (9 bores excluded), with EC values above it withheld as confidential.
steps.quote: this threshold value was set to delineate and discriminate against industrially impacted groundwater

steps.action: Check the premise that high EC is not natural, using the lack of evaporite indicators in the Urquhart Shale and the normal EC of along-strike bores away from the mine.
steps.quote: the bores along the north-south fault strike (and away from the mine area) do not have elevated EC despite being in the same formation

steps.action: Compare δ65Cu of the 9 unadulterated bores with distance to ore on the geological map and find values about 1.0–1.5‰ higher east of the Mount Isa Fault near the ore bodies.
steps.quote: display a clear trend towards higher δ65Cu values in lithologies east of the Mount Isa Fault hosting the Cu ore bodies

steps.action: Compute correlation matrices of δ65Cu and water parameters and read a weak positive δ65Cu–dO correlation as support for oxidative weathering.
steps.quote: The weakly positive δ65Cu—dO correlation further supports oxidative weathering as an operative mechanism

steps.action: Recompute the correlation matrices without the industrially impacted samples; the δ65Cu–dO and depth–dO correlations strengthen and a pH–EC correlation emerges.
steps.quote: the weak positive correlations for δ65Cu—dO and depth—dO are enhanced

steps.action: Explain the weakness of the δ65Cu–dO correlation with an auxiliary: Fe3+ in chalcopyrite can act as the oxidant instead of O2.
steps.quote: for this reason, the relationship between δ65Cu and dO is non-binary, again potentially explaining their weak correlation

steps.action: Compare bores one by one with mapped mineralization and bedrock Cu: low δ65Cu in southern bores without mineralization, high δ65Cu at Bore 45 near gossan; two rival sources are offered for Bore 33.
steps.quote: the strongly positive δ65Cu value is in excellent agreement with the documented mineralization

steps.action: Account for high δ65Cu at NB16/NB17, which sit above low-Cu bedrock, by fracture-controlled groundwater transport from the south, consistent with NE flow.
steps.quote: it is likely that the δ65Cu values indicate fracture-controlled ground water transported from the south

steps.action: Interpret high δ65Cu at Bores 31 and 30, where there is no surface mineralization, as tentative detection of hidden Cu mineralization; leave BSOC_B4 uninterpreted because it lies near a waste dump.
steps.quote: Result tentatively indicate significant detection of Cu mineralization in the absence of any surface mineralization.

steps.action: Take from experimental and field literature the expected fractionations: redox up to 3–4‰, and oxidative weathering of chalcopyrite +1.0–1.5‰.
steps.quote: oxidative weathering more generally produces +1.0–1.5‰ shift for chalcopyrite

steps.action: Compare groundwater δ65Cu near ore with the primary chalcopyrite baseline: a shift of about 1–2‰, matching the oxidative weathering expectation.
steps.quote: groundwater samples overlying or proximal to the main Cu-bearing mineralization at Mt Isa are shifted to higher δ65Cu by approximately 1–2‰

steps.action: Set aside adsorption (<1‰) and biological fractionation (would need unnaturally high bacterial densities) as dominant controls, using literature magnitudes.
steps.quote: but generally not at the same magnitude as the redox reactions described above

steps.action: Keep the claim that groundwater near ore at this sediment-hosted deposit is about 1‰ or more heavier than distal groundwater, driven by oxidative weathering of Cu sulfides.
steps.quote: display a clear trend towards strongly positive δ65Cu values (heavier Cu isotope compositions) in proximity to ore

steps.action: Refine the tool into a second use: Cu isotopes combined with EC to fingerprint industrial input; note that Cu isotopes alone cannot separate ore weathering from tailings.
steps.quote: the current work highlights not one, but two uses for Cu isotope systematics in hydrogeochemistry

steps.action: Combine the result with prior porphyry, exotic and IOCG studies to claim a consistent vector signature across deposit types.
steps.quote: groundwater Cu isotope compositions—thus far—provide a very consistent vector signature that can be used for Cu exploration

Yes: δ65Cu measured directly in groundwater and chalcopyrite
Test whether the Cu isotope vector works at a sediment-hosted deposit
Industrial input; adsorption or biological fractionation; groundwater transport; O2 versus Fe3+ oxidant
Partly: fractionation magnitudes from literature (oxidation 1–1.5‰, adsorption <1‰)
Found: known deposit and existing mine monitoring bores

tree.answer: Repetition only across 9 unadulterated bores at one deposit
Limited: analytical QC passed; correlations robust to the EC filter
Kept: positive δ65Cu excursion proximal to ore

end.claim: At the sediment-hosted Mount Isa deposit, unadulterated groundwater near Cu ore is about 1‰ or more heavier in δ65Cu than distal groundwater and 1–2‰ heavier than ore chalcopyrite, best explained by oxidative weathering of Cu sulfides, so groundwater Cu isotopes can vector to ore.

decisive_move.sentence: The comparison of δ65Cu in EC-filtered (unadulterated) bores against proximity to the known ore bodies is what produces the vector claim.

gates.evidence: Action: the study aim (test the Cu isotope vector at a known deposit) chose the site, but the samples are existing environmental monitoring bores collected by the mine's environmental department (p. 2-3). Claim: the trend could have been absent, but 9 of 18 bores were excluded by an EC threshold and BSOC_B4 by proximity to a waste dump, leaving 9 bores with no statistical test of the spatial trend (p. 4-6). Registration: the EC threshold comes from literature benchmarks (Naudet et al. 2004), but the paper does not say whether it was fixed before the data were seen (inference).

imports.item: Thermo Neptune Plus MC-ICP-MS with sample-standard bracketing
NIST SRM 976 Cu isotope reference standard
1838 USA penny in-house Cu standard (Mathur et al. 2009b)
EC benchmarks for freshwater versus industrial wastewater
first-principles oxidation states of chalcopyrite (Cu+ Fe3+)

novelty_claims.quote: as-of-yet have not been applied to any known sediment-hosted copper deposits as ground truth
the current work highlights not one, but two uses for Cu isotope systematics in hydrogeochemistry

limits:
Single deposit; only 9 unadulterated bores interpreted, and the spatial trend is read from a map with no statistical test or uncertainty. EC values above 5000 μS/cm2 are withheld as confidential, and data are available only on request. Internal inconsistencies:
- The text says five bores west of the fault had EC at or above 5000, then lists six, including BSOC_B4, whose reported EC is 1684.
- Bore 33 is said to have EC at or above 5000 yet is discussed among the low background bores.
- NB16 is given as 2.11 and 1.93‰ in the text but only 2.11 in Table 2.
- The Fig. 1 caption names sections 34500mN/345300 mN while Table 1 lists 34200N/35100N.

Excluding BSOC_B4 by proximity rather than by the EC rule, and explaining NB16/17 by groundwater transport, could be read as protective auxiliaries (inference). Rival mechanisms are excluded by literature magnitudes, not by tests performed here. Sub-claims and their statuses:
- Oxidative-weathering mechanism: best_explanation.
- EC plus Cu isotopes fingerprint industrial input: best_explanation, weakly supported.
- Tentative hidden mineralization at Bores 31 and 30: no status beyond 'tentatively indicate'.
- Generality across deposit types (synthesis with Kidder et al. and Mathur et al.): best_explanation.

The work is funded by the mine operator and a co-author is a mine employee. No review file was supplied, so the review history is unknown.

disagreements.target: trace-metal concentration hydrogeochemical exploration (e.g. Kidder et al. 2022a; Eppinger et al. 2013)
disagreements.support: The paper argues that element profiles depend on water-rock partitioning and water chemistry and give non-unique results, citing Mathur et al. 2013 that Cu concentrations do not track proximity.
disagreements.quote: a fundamental caveat of this approach is that trace element profiles are beholden to water-mineral/rock partitioning

disagreements.target: geophysics as the go-to next-generation exploration method
disagreements.support: The paper notes cost, false positives from conductive materials, and sensitivity loss with depth; no data are offered.
disagreements.quote: are not only susceptible to false positives generated by other electromagnetically active materials

disagreements.target: multi-proxy approaches of Mathur et al. 2013 and Kidder et al. 2021, 2022b
disagreements.support: The Mount Isa result is offered as evidence that Cu isotopes plus EC suffice for a first-order vector.
disagreements.quote: are all that is required in order to construct a first-order vector to Cu-bearing ore

alternatives_considered.alternatives: freshwater range 100–2000 and industrial wastewater ~10,000 μS/cm2 benchmarks
alternatives_considered.reason: previous observations that EC above ~5000 indicates industrially impacted water (Naudet et al. 2004)

alternatives_considered.chosen: chalcopyrite from within or directly above the main ore body
alternatives_considered.reason: to minimize secondary effects such as Rayleigh distillation away from primary deposition

alternatives_considered.chosen: correlation matrices for both all samples and unadulterated samples only
alternatives_considered.reason: to compare with and without industrially impacted waters

alternatives_considered.chosen: both O2 and Fe3+ as possible oxidants
alternatives_considered.reason: chalcopyrite stoichiometry Cu+Fe3+S2 allows Fe3+ reduction

alternatives_considered.alternatives: Lena prospect pyrite-rich gossan versus drainage from the Bernborough Lead mine for Bore 33
alternatives_considered.reason: relatively low pH perhaps supports mine drainage

alternatives_considered.chosen: fracture-controlled groundwater transported from the south
alternatives_considered.reason: bedrock Cu below 65 ppm, NE flow direction, lower δ65Cu than Bore 45
bore is only 250 m from a waste dump
adsorption gives <1‰; biological overprint needs bacterial densities above natural levels
